findings.title: Policy Address signals future consultation on AI-enabled fraudulent content

rendered_html: 📔 Regulatory Bulletin — 17 September 2026 (Daily) Executive Summary • The Hong Kong Government signals a later-2026 public consultation on a framework intended to encourage technology and telecommunications sectors to detect and remove potentially fraudulent online content, including AI-generated content. It creates no current bank obligation or HKMA requirement, but merits monitoring for future payment-fraud, customer-communication and third-party-interface implications. Hong Kong 🟡 Policy Address signals future consultation on AI-enabled fraudulent content 🇭🇰 Item ID: item-20260916-daily-exploratory-search-bebee74ebf ⏰ Deadline: Later in 2026 (public consultation; exact date not stated) Products: Payments, Digital channels The Government's 16 September Policy Address says the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau will conduct a public consultation later in 2026 on expanding the legal framework to encourage technology and telecommunications sectors to improve detection and removal of potentially fraudulent online content, including content generated through AI misuse. The announcement gives no consultation paper, exact consultation date, final legal scope, implementation date or bank duty. It does not establish a current bank obligation or HKMA requirement; however, digital-payment customers may remain exposed to AI-enabled scam content while the policy develops. Fraud-risk and Legal/Compliance teams should log the consultation for horizon scanning and, once published, make an applicability decision covering affected payment journeys, customer harm, data/privacy and external-provider dependencies, retaining the decision and monitoring evidence. Source: Full text of the Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address (4) SG/UK/GLOBAL Benchmark Comparable overseas developments and commercial/control benchmarks. They do not establish Hong Kong requirements. Watch List • Monitor publication of the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau consultation and assess applicability only when its proposed scope, affected entities and any information-sharing provisions are available.
